questions.question: Two sibling React components must stay in sync. Where should their state live?
questions.title: Lifting shared state to one owner
questions.direct_answer: Move the shared state to the siblings' closest common parent. The parent passes the current value down through props and passes callbacks that let each child request an update. This lifting-state-up pattern creates one source of truth. Keep unrelated local details inside the children and move state higher only if more consumers genuinely need it.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can resolve synchronization with ownership instead of mirror Effects.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Keeping duplicate state in both siblings and trying to copy changes between them.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Choose the nearest owner, derive alternate representations, and explain the remaining local state.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Find the closest common parent of all components that need the value.
Store one state value in that parent.
Pass current data down as props.
Pass event callbacks down so children can request changes.
Keep unrelated child state local.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
When sibling components must show and change the same information, I give that information one owner. I find their closest common parent, move the shared state there, and pass the current value to both children as props. This is lifting state up.

The children do not directly modify the parent's state. The parent passes callback props such as `onValueChange`, and a child calls the callback from its event handler. The parent updates its state, renders again, and both siblings receive props derived from the same new snapshot.

For example, Celsius and Fahrenheit inputs should not each keep an independent temperature and use Effects to copy values. The parent can store one temperature plus the scale last edited. It converts that source value during render and passes a matching display value to each controlled input.

This design prevents loops and drift. With duplicate state, rounding or a missed update can make the fields disagree. With one owner, every render calculates both displays from one fact, and one edit follows a clear path from child event to parent update to new child props.

I lift only the state that is actually shared. Focus state, a local validation message, or whether one input's help text is open can remain inside that input if no sibling depends on it. If a more distant part of the application later needs the temperature, I reassess the owner rather than automatically placing everything in a global store. The practical answer is one source of truth at the nearest common owner, values down through props, and change requests up through callbacks. Derived representations stay calculations instead of becoming more synchronized state.

sections.title: Synchronization becomes ownership
sections.content: Two copies require rules for keeping each other current. One owner turns that problem into ordinary data flow: an event reaches the owner, and the resulting value flows back to every consumer.

sections.title: Why mirror Effects form a loop
sections.content:
If Celsius state updates Fahrenheit state in one Effect and Fahrenheit updates Celsius in another, each state change can trigger another conversion. Even when equality stops the loop, rounding and intermediate renders make the relationship difficult to reason about.

A common owner stores the independent fact and calculates both views in one render. Conversion functions remain plain and testable. The component tree now documents who is responsible for consistency.

sections.title: One edit updates both siblings
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Celsius input event] --> B[Converter parent state]
  B --> C[derive Celsius prop]
  B --> D[derive Fahrenheit prop]
  C --> E[Celsius input]
  D --> F[Fahrenheit input]
```

sections.title: Control both inputs from the parent
Boundary to remember
sections.content: A common parent is not automatically the application root. Lifting state too high makes unrelated areas render around and depend on state they do not own. Start with the lowest parent that contains all real consumers.

questions.question: A todo was changed, but the React UI did not update correctly. How would you find the mutation bug?
questions.title: Debugging mutated React state
questions.direct_answer: Check whether code changed an object or array already held in state and then reused its reference. Reproduce one update, compare references before and after, and inspect mutating operations such as assignment, `push`, `splice`, `sort`, or `reverse`. Fix it by returning replacement objects and arrays, copying every changed nested level, then add a regression test.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can connect an incorrect update to reference reuse and damaged snapshots.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Spreading an outer object after its nested object was already mutated.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use reference checks and frozen test fixtures to prove the repair.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Reproduce one action with a tiny state value.
Look for direct assignment and mutating array methods.
Check both outer and changed nested references.
Return a new array and a new object for the changed todo.
Verify old state remains unchanged after the update.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I would first reduce the bug to one todo and one user action, then inspect the state update rather than assuming React failed to render. Objects and arrays in state are JavaScript references, so code can change their contents while still passing React the same outer value.

I would search the update path for property assignment and mutating methods such as `push`, `splice`, `sort`, or `reverse`. I would also check nested references. `{ ...state }` is only a shallow copy; if the code changed `state.todos[0].done` first, the old and new outer objects still share an already-mutated todo.

For example, `todos[0].done = true; setTodos(todos)` changes the current array in place and gives the setter that same array. The correct update maps the array and returns a new todo object only for the matching ID. React receives a replacement array, and earlier snapshots are not rewritten.

During debugging I can log reference comparisons such as `nextTodos === todos` and `nextTodos[0] === todos[0]`. For a changed first item, both should be false; unchanged items may correctly keep the same reference. React DevTools can confirm the state value and which component owns it.

I would add a focused test that starts from a frozen fixture, performs the transition, checks the next visible result, and verifies the original fixture did not change. Freezing in development or tests can turn silent mutation into an immediate error, though it is not a substitute for a clear update function. Finally I would check the state shape. If every update requires several fragile nested copies, flattening records by ID or moving transitions to a reducer can make the legal change explicit and reduce future mutation bugs.

sections.title: Prove whether the reference or the data changed
sections.content: A useful mutation investigation separates content equality from reference identity. React updates are expressed by next snapshots; changing the current snapshot first makes the before-and-after comparison unreliable.

sections.title: Track the changed path only
sections.content:
For `board.columns[2].cards[4].done`, a correct immutable update needs a new board, columns array, changed column, cards array, and changed card. Siblings outside that path can retain their references.

This structural sharing is both correct and efficient. Copying every nested object wastes work; mutating one shared nested object corrupts old state. The update should replace exactly the path whose value changed.

sections.title: Expected identity after toggling todo A
sections.content:
old array ≠ new array
old todo A ≠ new todo A
old todo B = new todo B
old array contents remain unchanged

sections.title: Replace the changed todo
Boundary to remember
sections.content: A UI that stays stale can also have a wrong event handler, an incorrect condition, or state owned in an unexpected component. Reference checks diagnose mutation specifically; they should be combined with tracing the event and inspecting the actual state owner.

followup_questions: Why is object spread not enough for every nested update?
Which JavaScript array methods mutate their receiver?
How can a reducer make complex state updates easier to test?

questions.question: Why does a React event handler run during render instead of on click?
questions.title: Passing React event handlers correctly
questions.direct_answer: The handler runs during render when JSX calls it, as in `onClick={saveOrder()}`. React needs a function value to call later, so pass `onClick={saveOrder}` or an inline function such as `onClick={() => saveOrder(order.id)}`. Calling a state setter while rendering can then create a re-render loop.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner distinguishes passing a callback from evaluating a function expression.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing `onClick={setOpen(true)}` and triggering state updates while React is rendering.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Trace when the JSX expression is evaluated and when the returned callback is invoked.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: JSX event props receive a function, not the result of calling one.
Use `onClick={handleClick}` when no extra argument is needed.
Use an inline function when arguments must be supplied later.
React calls the handler after the browser event, not during render.
A setter called during render can cause a repeated-render error.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A React event prop such as `onClick` expects a function that React can call when the event happens. If JSX contains `onClick={saveOrder()}`, JavaScript evaluates `saveOrder()` immediately while the component is rendering and assigns its return value to `onClick`. React never received the original function for the later click.

When the handler needs no extra argument, I pass the function itself: `onClick={saveOrder}`. When it needs an argument, I create a function without calling the action yet: `onClick={() => saveOrder(order.id)}`. React receives that arrow function and invokes it after the user clicks.

For example, `onClick={setOpen(true)}` calls the state setter during every render. The setter queues another render, which calls the setter again, and React eventually reports too many re-renders. `onClick={() => setOpen(true)}` delays the setter until the browser click is handled.

The browser event is passed as the first argument when React invokes a handler. A named function can receive it directly, such as `function handleSubmit(event)`. An inline function can receive the event and add application data, for example `event => removeItem(item.id, event)`.

Passing an inline function is not automatically a performance problem. It does create a new function during rendering, but that matters only in a measured case where referential equality affects a memoized child or another dependency. Correct timing and readable arguments come first. The core distinction is expression result versus callback value. JSX evaluates the expression inside braces during render. That expression must produce the function React should save for later, not perform the user action while the screen is being calculated.

sections.title: Pass now, call later
sections.content: Event props separate render time from interaction time. Rendering creates the callback value; React stores it with the element; a later browser event causes React to invoke it.

sections.title: Braces always evaluate an expression
sections.content:
Both `{saveOrder}` and `{saveOrder()}` are JavaScript expressions. The first evaluates to a function object. The second evaluates by calling the function and produces whatever that call returns—often `undefined`. The syntax difference determines timing.

An inline arrow also evaluates immediately, but evaluating it creates a function rather than executing its body. The body runs only when the created function is called. This is why it can capture an item ID for a future event.

sections.title: What JSX gives to onClick
sections.content:
| JSX | Evaluated during render | Called on click |
|---|---|---|
| `onClick={saveOrder}` | The `saveOrder` function | `saveOrder(event)` |
| `onClick={() => saveOrder(id)}` | A new arrow function | Arrow calls `saveOrder(id)` |
| `onClick={saveOrder()}` | The function's return value | Usually nothing callable |

sections.title: Delay actions until the click
Boundary to remember
sections.content: A handler passed to a custom component is only a prop until that component attaches or invokes it. Naming callback props with an `on` prefix communicates that they represent events, but React does not automatically wire arbitrary custom props to the browser.

questions.question: A React search shows results for an older query. How would you prevent the stale response?
questions.title: Preventing stale search responses
questions.direct_answer: Each query starts asynchronous work that may finish out of order. In the Effect cleanup, abort the previous fetch with an `AbortController`, or mark that Effect instance as ignored and refuse to update state after cleanup. Include the query in dependencies, handle empty queries explicitly, and let only the current request publish results.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner recognizes an asynchronous race instead of blaming state batching.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Fetching on every query without cleanup and allowing the last response to win regardless of which query it belongs to.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Trace two requests completing out of order and distinguish aborting work from ignoring its completion.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Responses can finish in a different order from requests.
Tie each request lifetime to the query Effect that started it.
Cleanup should abort or ignore the previous request.
Only the current Effect may set results or errors.
Framework loaders or query libraries can manage caching and cancellation at scale.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The bug is a race between requests. Typing `re` can start request A and quickly typing `react` can start request B. If B finishes first and A finishes later, an unguarded A callback overwrites the current results with data for the older query.

I tie each request to the Effect instance created for its query. The query is a dependency, so a new query causes cleanup of the previous instance before setup starts the next request. Cleanup can call `AbortController.abort()` for `fetch`, which signals that the earlier work is no longer needed.

For example, setup creates a controller, fetches `/search?q=react` with its signal, and sets results only on success. Cleanup aborts that controller. The catch path ignores `AbortError` but records real network failures. The request for the current query remains active because it has its own controller.

For an asynchronous API that cannot be aborted, I use an `ignore` boolean closed over by that Effect. Cleanup sets it to true, and the completion checks `if (!ignore)` before updating state. This does not save network work, but it prevents an obsolete completion from changing the screen.

I also handle an empty query without making a request, represent loading and error states deliberately, and encode the query with `URLSearchParams` rather than string concatenation. In development I test with delayed responses so the older request intentionally finishes last. For a production application, a framework loader or a query library may provide deduplication, caching, server rendering, and cancellation. The invariant remains the same: only data belonging to the current query may become the current result.

sections.title: Latest request is not always latest response
sections.content: Networks preserve neither speed nor completion order. UI state needs a relevance rule based on the query that initiated work, not on whichever promise happens to resolve last.

sections.title: Two valid cancellation strategies
sections.content:
Aborting asks a compatible operation to stop and causes `fetch` to reject with an abort-related error. Ignoring allows the work to finish but blocks its callback from publishing. Some systems need both because cancellation may be advisory or arrive after a response has already completed.

Loading state also belongs to a request lifetime. Cleanup or the new setup must prevent request A's `finally` block from marking request B as finished. A request ID or query-library state machine can make that ownership explicit for more complex flows.

sections.title: Out-of-order completion
sections.content:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant A as Request re
  participant B as Request react
  participant S as UI state
  U->>A: type re
  U->>B: type react; cleanup aborts A
  B-->>S: publish react results
  A--xS: aborted result cannot publish
```

sections.title: Abort the request owned by the old query
Boundary to remember
sections.content: Client Effects do not provide caching, server rendering, retry policy, or request deduplication automatically. For route data or widely shared server state, use the data-loading system chosen by the application's framework or a well-tested query library.
